criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water and wastewater service access disparities affecting First Nations, Inuit, and Métis communities in Canada (lack of piped water, truck delivery, potable dispensing units, and reliance on untreated surface water).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — discusses decentralised water governance in Canada, neo-liberal governance, constitutional obligations (Sections 35 and 36), the Indian Act, the First Nations Water Management Strategy, and the 2012 Safe Drinking Water for First Nations Act. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — the paper's core analytical focus is macro-governance, settler-colonial national identity, and neo-liberalism as ideological background rather than an analysis of a rule-type mechanism directly governing access (although it mentions in passing from secondary sources that federal water strategies/statutes exclude off-reserve/Inuit/Métis communities and expect 20% community cost contributions, these are not empirically analysed as mechanisms). Under both readings, the paper is excluded for lacking empirical evidence (c3 = no, E05).
criterion_notes.c3: NO — conceptual/theoretical essay and narrative overview with no primary data collection, no empirical methodology, and no systematic review/synthesis protocol. The 'five short case studies' (pp. 76-79) are single-paragraph illustrative vignettes summarizing previously published studies and news reports (Goldhar et al. 2014; Hanrahan et al. 2015; Walters et al. 2012; La Rose 2007; Jacobs et al. 2010). Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Cites secondary access and exclusion outcomes (e.g., Indigenous households being 90 times more likely to lack piped water, 28% of on-reserve houses lacking piped water, boil-water advisories, and intermittent operation of a potable dispensing water unit), though none are primary empirical findings of this article.
criterion_notes.c5: NO — because this is a non-empirical theoretical/narrative essay drawing on secondary statistics and brief literature vignettes, there is no identifiable empirical study design, primary sample, or operationalized exposure-outcome analysis.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with bilingual English and French abstracts).

evidence_quotes.quote: Indigenous people are ninety times more likely than other Canadians to lack piped water.

Five short case studies of water insecurity demonstrate how neo-liberalism props up and legitimises decentralised water governance in Canada, which in turn promotes and maintains environmental inequality, Indigenous marginalisation and, ultimately, the Canadian identity.
In this article I argue that Indigenous exclusion, an outgrowth of the settler myths that are woven into Canadian identity, is the bedrock factor in maintaining Indigenous water insecurity.
There is no national unified water governance system, no national enforceable drinking water standards and no standardised measures for water governance.
A sample of case studies demonstrates the variety of water insecurity experiences across Indigenous Canada; two Inuit and three First Nations communities are featured.
In fact, 28 per cent of houses on First Nations reserves lack piped water with 13.5 per cent using truck delivery (Statistics Canada 2012).

raw_response.exposure: Canadian national identity, settler colonialism, neo-liberalism, and decentralised water governance (macro-governance/ideological critique; briefly notes reserve-only statutory scope and 20% community cost-sharing expectations from secondary literature)
raw_response.outcome: Community and household drinking-water and wastewater insecurity (lack of piped water, reliance on truck delivery or untreated surface water, boil-water advisories, and water contamination cited from secondary sources)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Indigenous peoples (First Nations, Inuit, and Métis communities) in Canada discussed via secondary national statistics and five one-paragraph secondary-literature vignettes (no primary sample)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the article addresses Indigenous household and community water/wastewater access disparities in Canada, it is a conceptual and narrative essay arguing that settler-colonial national identity and neo-liberalism sustain Indigenous water insecurity. It reports no primary empirical data, no empirical research methods, and no systematic synthesis protocol; its 'five short case studies' are one-paragraph vignettes summarizing previously published papers and a newspaper report. Additionally, under the 2026-10-13 narrow reading of Criterion 2, its central focus is macro-governance/ideological background rather than empirical analysis of a specific rule-type access mechanism. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper remains excluded due to the absence of empirical evidence (E05).
raw_response.study_design: Theoretical and narrative essay with brief secondary-source vignettes (non-empirical)
